concept.name: Tracking error
concept.definition: The standard deviation of a portfolio's active return relative to its benchmark — also called active risk — measuring how closely the portfolio follows its index. Measured historically it is ex post (realized) tracking error; model-predicted it is ex ante tracking error.
concept.intuition: It is the wobble between you and the index: an index fund hugs the benchmark (tracking error near zero) while an aggressive active manager wanders far from it.
concept.mechanics: Compute the active return series (portfolio minus benchmark) and take its standard deviation; in factor-model terms it is the non-systematic (residual) risk, and in weight space it equals sqrt((w_p - w_b)' Sigma (w_p - w_b)). Dividing mean active return by tracking error gives the information ratio.
concept.formula: TE = sqrt( var(r_p - r_b) ) = sqrt( (w_p - w_b)' Sigma (w_p - w_b) ), where r_p and r_b are portfolio and benchmark returns and (w_p - w_b) the vector of active weights.
concept.failure_modes: Ex ante estimates from factor models can diverge from realized values by large factors when the model misses risks, and TE measured over benign windows understates active risk in regime shifts. A low-TE 'active' fund may simply be a closet indexer charging active fees.
concept.misconceptions: Tracking error is not a mistake or failure — for index funds it should be minimal, but for active mandates a larger TE is the deliberate price of seeking alpha — and it excludes market-direction risk, measuring only deviation from the benchmark.
concept.example: An active equity fund whose monthly returns deviate from its benchmark with a standard deviation of 0.67% has a tracking error of about 0.67% * sqrt(12), roughly 2.3% annualized.
